analysis.one_liner: Raises legal barriers to forming and keeping a union, while adding union-election, dues, and strike-vote rules.
analysis.headline: The Employee Rights Act never got a vote: referred to the Senate labor committee in November 2013 with 28 Republican cosponsors, it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the nation's basic labor law in ways that make it substantially harder for workers to form a union and much harder for a union to keep representing a workforce. It would require that union elections be won by a majority of all employees in a workplace, not just those who vote, so employees who stay home count as 'no' votes. It would force unions to win fresh recertification elections whenever more than half a workforce turns over, require a majority of all affected employees to approve any strike in a vote run by an organization the employer helps choose, and let employees' dues be spent on anything beyond bargaining only with a written, annually renewed opt-in. It also bundles in some genuine worker protections, such as letting nonmembers vote on contract ratification, requiring unions to share audited finances, and adding penalties for union coercion of workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially those who want to avoid or shed unions, benefit from a slower election process and rules that make union representation fragile. Workers who oppose union representation at their workplace benefit, since a majority of all employees (including non-voters) must support the union, and existing units can be forced into recertification votes. Union nonmembers gain voting rights on contract ratification and strikes, the right to opt out of funding non-bargaining union activity, and access to union audit reports.

how_it_helps.text: Every employee in a represented unit, whether or not they join the union, would get the same right as members to vote by secret ballot on ratifying a contract or going on strike [S2][S3].
Union dues could not be spent on anything not directly related to collective bargaining unless the employee authorizes it in writing, with no automatic renewal after one year [S2][S3].
Unions would have to make an independently verified annual audit of their finances available to members and to represented nonmembers [S2][S3].

A union found to have coerced employees — including over a decertification petition — would owe lost wages, unlawfully collected dues, and liquidated damages, and could not file objections to the resulting election [S2][S3].

Using force, violence, or threats to obtain representation rights or employment terms would carry criminal penalties of up to $100,000 in fines and 10 years in prison, and union conduct constituting extortion could not be excused because of the union's lawful goals [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Unions and the workers who rely on them bear the cost. The majority-of-all-employees rule counts every non-voter against the union, the recertification trigger puts representation up for a vote after ordinary workforce turnover, pre-election hearings and appeals stretch out the process, and the strike-vote and dues rules cut both union leverage and union funding.

drawbacks.text: Requiring a majority of all employees in the unit, rather than of those voting, treats every employee who abstains as a 'no' vote — a standard no candidate would accept in their own election [S2][S3].

The bill forces a recertification election whenever more than 50% of a unit's employees turn over, and directs that the election proceed 'without regard to the pendency of any unfair labor practice charge against the employer' — meaning a union could be voted out even while the employer faces pending charges of illegal conduct [S3].

No strike could begin without majority approval of all affected employees in a vote run by a 'neutral, private organization' chosen by agreement between the employer and the union, and if the employer has made an offer, employees must vote on that offer before voting to strike — with the union paying election costs — which shifts leverage toward employers during negotiations [S2][S3].

New hearing and appeal requirements before any election, plus a rule that results are not final until the NLRB resolves every issue, would lengthen an election process that employers and unions alike already criticize for delay [S2][S3].
The penalties for coercion apply to labor organizations only; the bill adds no comparable damages remedy against employers that illegally coerce employees [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The union-democracy provisions — nonmember voting rights, dues transparency, audited finances, penalties for coercion — are real and would appeal to workers who want more say in or less money flowing to their union. But they are bundled with structural changes that tilt the field heavily: silence counts as a vote against the union, routine workforce turnover can cost a union its certification, strikes require employer-influenced supermajority votes, and union political spending is subject to annual opt-in. An honest reading is that the genuine protections are the smaller part of the bill; the larger effect is to make organizing and keeping a union much harder.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, which never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on November 14, 2013, joined by 24 original Republican cosponsors including McConnell, Paul, and Rubio; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1][S3][S5].
It ultimately drew 28 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record — and the bill received no floor action before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the workers who count on collective bargaining are better off that the bill died, since its main provisions would have made organizing harder and existing representation easier to lose. Employers gained nothing directly, but they also avoided no cost; the status quo on labor law was preserved.

for.name: Sen. Orrin G. Hatch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Employee Rights Act in the Senate.

against.name: Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup, leaving it to die in committee at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic chairman of the committee with jurisdiction never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would cut union revenue through the dues opt-in, force repeated recertification elections triggered by ordinary turnover, require supermajority strike votes run at union expense, and slow the election process — all shrinking unions' ability to organize and bargain. It also adds provisions some union members genuinely want: nonmember voting on contracts and strikes, audited finances, and penalties for union coercion of workers.

industries.industry: Employers, particularly nonunion businesses and union-avoidance consultants
industries.note: Longer election timelines, a majority-of-all-employees standard, and mandatory recertification votes make it harder and costlier for workers to organize, which lowers the risk of unionization for employers. That gain comes directly at the expense of workers' bargaining power, not alongside it.
